speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for Digital Development and Information)
text: Can I get permission to take Question Nos 5 and 6 together, please?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And my reply will also address related questions from Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Louis Chua filed for tomorrow's Sitting.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If the Members are satisfied with the response, they may wish to withdraw their questions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We share the Members' concerns and have been tracking these developments closely for some time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government does not have access to Mythos.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: More broadly, we do not assume that we will always have early access to every frontier model.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Instead, we maintain close working relationships with various partners, including major artificial intelligence (AI) labs and cybersecurity firms to track capability developments and to assess safety and security implications when new capabilities emerge.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are also working with partners who have access to Mythos to better understand its capabilities and implications.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We should understand the advances in capabilities enabled by Mythos to be part of a continuum rather than a step change.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Models like OpenAI's GPT-5.5 already show comparable cybersecurity capabilities and are more widely available.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Open-source AI models are also rapidly improving and are likely to reach similar capabilities within months.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: With AI, vulnerabilities that once took expert teams weeks to detect manually can now be identified autonomously in hours, sometimes minutes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities much faster than our traditional patching cycles can address.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: AI is also changing how attacks are carried out.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, Google reported in 2025 that threat actors had used AI to develop a new class of malware.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Unlike traditional malware that is hard-coded at the point of creation, the PROMPTFLUX malware was designed to consult a live AI model during attacks.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The AI would rewrite portions of the malware code in real-time to evade detection.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Similar attempts have been made against business executives internationally and in Singapore too.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, voice cloning requires only seconds of audio and impersonation tools are readily available.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These attacks are faster, more scalable and significantly more sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: What we have not yet seen is fully autonomous AI agents running end-to-end campaigns.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But this is a matter of time given the trajectory of technological developments.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, the issue is not any single model like Mythos.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The underlying shift is broader and the risks are real.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are treating them with the seriousness they deserve.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To Mr Saktiandi Supaat's query, we view AI-enabled cyber risk as an amplification of an existing systemic risk, rather than a wholly new category.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The fundamentals to strengthen an organisation's cybersecurity matters more than ever.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Therefore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has convened the chief executive officers of major financial institutions to discuss the threat landscape and drive collective action on technology and cyber resilience.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Financial institutions are treating this with the seriousness it deserves and have been strengthening their posture.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This letter sets out clear expectations, including a review of cyber risk posture in light of AI-enabled threats.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is not an issue that should be delegated to IT teams alone.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It demands leadership attention at the highest levels, including board members and chief executives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This applies whether an organisation runs information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), or both types of systems.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The priority is to get the fundamentals right – and do so quickly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Update these for IT and OT systems to account for the AI-enabled changes in the threat environment – in particular, the narrowing window between the discovery of a vulnerability and its exploitation by attackers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Most breaches begin at an unmanaged asset – a forgotten internet-facing system, a third-party dependency, a shadow cloud account.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ensure you have visibility over your current inventory.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The time window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation is collapsing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Organisations need to move towards continuous monitoring, automated detection and tested incident response.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: AI tools introduce new vulnerabilities, particularly when connected to sensitive data, code or critical systems.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The same capabilities adversaries are deploying can be turned to detection, triaging and response.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether the Government is investing in AI-powered tools for active vulnerability and patch testing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government has been fast-tracking capability building in using AI for cybersecurity for some time, working with industry to access and adapt the best tools available globally.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we are developing capabilities in-house, so that we are not dependent on any single external party.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These are being piloted within Government and will be extended to more agencies and CII owners when ready.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Under the Cybersecurity Act, CSA has the authority to direct and enforce action where necessary.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we assess the risk based on published evaluations, threat intelligence and our ongoing engagement with the major AI labs.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Where credible evidence emerges of a material risk to systems of national consequence, we work with and advise CII owners to patch and harden their systems.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is the approach we have used to date and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about early warning indicators and triggers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have an established approach to do this.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, we closely engage technology partners for early visibility and insights into new capabilities as they emerge.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, CSA monitors active exploitation patterns and shares threat intelligence and advisories through established channels.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, we conduct attack-surface monitoring and increasingly we are leveraging AI to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about patching protocols and timelines.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There are established practices for patching that can manage disruption to services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes staged rollouts and pre-tested roll-back procedures.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These efforts form a broader national effort to raise cybersecurity standards across all sectors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There is no silver bullet and no one-time fixes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We must adapt and adjust to new risks.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This requires all stakeholders to play their part actively and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Many small and medium enterprises (SMEs) do not have a chief information security officer (CISO) or even a dedicated IT team.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes the CISO-as-a-Service and the Cyber Essentials and Cyber Trust Marks, which support organisations to assess and improve their security posture.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Individuals have a role to play as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Three things matter most, as outlined in CSA's "Stop and Check" campaign.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, update software promptly to ensure that cyber criminals cannot find and use vulnerabilities to infect devices with malware, steal data or take control of devices.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, use ScamShield and anti-virus to safeguard devices and accounts.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But resilience depends on everyone doing their part.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We must act early and decisively and stay ahead of the threat.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First of all, frontier models require a significant amount of compute and are likely to be concentrated among well-resourced organisations, leading to concerns about accessibility and uneven capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this context, my first supplementary question is whether Singapore is actually working with international partners to establish norms, safeguards and coordinated responses to the risk posed by frontier AI models in cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second supplementary question is whether the cybersecurity framework today, including those under the Cybersecurity Act and the CSA guidelines, are sufficient to address these emerging threats?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And third, most importantly, how will the Government ensure that SMEs are not left behind and have access to these emerging new frontier capabilities to defend against such threats?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I mentioned earlier, the enhanced capabilities that frontier models bring to the table is on a continuum.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have been monitoring this for some time and we have been taking steps to mitigate the risk.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The second is that – I will go back to the same point I made earlier – fundamentals matter.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As an organisation or an individual, you lock the front door, or you secure the locks of your front door when you leave the building or when you leave your house.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But over time, when we adopt more digital solutions, digital devices, adopt more different services in our organisation, even in our personal lives, we are almost thinking about it like building more annexes and building more facilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Which means that your attack surface is much wider because you might have forgotten that you might have left a window open, your back door open, or a new annex in your building has a vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And what AI empowers or enables the bad actors to do is this that makes them much more capable and much faster in detecting those vulnerabilities and exploiting them.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, first and foremost, it is about securing your own building, your own house, your own organisation, your own digital systems, making sure that vulnerabilities are detected early and locked down.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And put in place enough investments to maintain your property, your digital systems, so that these vulnerabilities would not be exploited by others.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, basic hygiene matters, and I spoke about it extensively in my Parliamentary Question reply.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And through programmes like SMEs Go Digital, where we work with our industry partners providing these technology solutions and pre-approve them for support, we make sure those basic cybersecurity hygiene practices are baked into those systems.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, we are taking a holistic view on it.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But these threats are not new and we have been monitoring them for some time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that cyber threats, especially AI-driven ones, are really borderless and driven by highly sophisticated global actors, could the Senior Minister of State clarify whether Singapore faces constraint in attracting and retaining top-tier global cybersecurity and AI talent needed to safeguard our systems?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How confident is the Government that we have sufficient depth of experience and expertise to protect critical infrastructure and maintain public trust, rather than falling behind more advanced threat actors?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I cannot agree more with him that talent is the most critical piece in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As we talk about adopting AI, it is important for us also to adopt AI as the good guys, the defenders – how are we building capabilities in AI to detect, to triage, to respond across the board.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But there is no one singular definition of what kind of cybersecurity talent is needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is a whole spectrum – from running operations to detection, to be able to do red teaming and penetration testing to sniff out vulnerabilities before the bad actors can do that.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And in fact, I read a quite useful article yesterday in CNA about talent, and we are doing much more.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, if anyone is keen to have a career in cybersecurity, please check out the resources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just three quick supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, I think the Senior Minister of State talks about gaining access to the best tools available globally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, I think the Senior Minister of State also talked about how it is working with partners that actually have access.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I was wondering if there has been any outcomes or patches to threats and vulnerabilities that have already been done, and if there have been any successes that the Senior Minister of State can share.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And lastly, in terms of the level of risk assessment through the CII, what is the Government's assessment of it right now, and how is it directly supporting the CII providers other than getting them to take action right now?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Because this is a trend that we have seen for some time, and we have been monitoring the trend and taking action for period of time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And it is not just about a single model but broadly, even open-source models, we have built up capabilities over time and within matter of months because of how fast AI technology is developing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We work closely with all AI labs, cybersecurity firms as well as different partners around the world to have early access, if we can, to different models and frontier models to test the capabilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, this is something we are working on.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On his second question around our risk assessment, well, we have been monitoring this trend for some time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Over the last months and year, we have been issuing different advisories.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Some of them we publish and are publicly available, like how we think about securing agentic AI software systems in our organisations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And the reason why I do so is to personally engage the leadership of each CII sector to understand what they are doing and to reinforce the threat that we are seeing because of AI capabilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And I am very heartened that all the senior leadership, from chief executives to board members, are aware of the risks and are taking steps.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They are putting in place, not just processes and investments to secure themselves and their systems, but also proactively thinking about how to secure their AI uses in their organisations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When you want to have a fast car, you have a strong engine under the hood of your car.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: You want to get from point A to point B as quickly as possible to be competitive.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But at the same time, you need to have the safety features, the guardrails, your safety belts, good brakes in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And organisations are thinking about how to secure the AI solutions in their organisations, even as they think about using AI to defend.
